questions.q: Why might a column of numbers load as 'object' (text) instead of a numeric type?
options: Source issues like a stray currency symbol, inconsistent formatting, or a source system quoting every value as a string
Only if the DataFrame has more than 1000 rows
Pandas always converts every column to numeric automatically
This can never actually happen with numeric data
questions.explain: Real-world source data quirks — quoting, formatting, stray symbols — can cause a genuinely numeric column to load as text, showing as 'object' in .dtypes.

questions.q: What happens if you try to .sum() a numeric-looking column that's actually stored as text?
options: Pandas automatically converts it to numeric first, so the sum is always correct
It silently produces string concatenation instead of numeric addition, rather than throwing an obvious error
The column is automatically dropped from the DataFrame
It always throws a clear error immediately
questions.explain: This is the dangerous part — text 'addition' concatenates characters rather than adding values, which can silently produce nonsense that looks plausible at a glance.

options: Removes all non-numeric characters from a column without converting its type
Only works on columns that are already numeric
Converts a column to text
Converts a column to the integer data type
questions.explain: astype(int) explicitly converts a column's data type — turning the string '120' into the actual integer 120, so mathematical operations work correctly.

questions.q: What habit does this lesson recommend for any freshly loaded dataset?
options: Immediately delete any column that contains numbers
Skip type checking entirely and only check for missing values
Convert every column to text regardless of its actual content
Check .dtypes first, before filtering, grouping, or calculating anything
questions.explain: Checking .dtypes as a first step — before any other operation — catches type mismatches early, before they cause quiet miscalculations downstream.

questions.q: In the lesson's example, what does Units Sold summing to 205 confirm?
options: That the original text values were correct all along
That the DataFrame has exactly 205 rows
That the column was successfully converted to a real numeric type using .astype(int), since 120 + 85 = 205
That .astype() failed and fell back to string concatenation
questions.explain: 205 is the correct numeric sum of 120 and 85 — confirming the conversion worked, since summing the original string values would have concatenated them instead.
